plan.contextChunk:
One classical example of the limitations of motion estimation from
images is the **aperture problem**. The aperture problem happens when
observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the
image frame, as shown in @fig-apperture_problem. If none of the
termination points are in view within the observation window (i.e., the
aperture), it is impossible to measure the actual image motion. Only the
component orthogonal to the moving structure can be measured.

![Aperture problem when observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the image frame. The actual motion of the bar is upward, but the perception, when vision is limited to what is visible within the observation window, appears as if the motion of the bar is in the direction perpendicular to the bar.](figures/optical_flow/apperture_problem.png){width="100%" #fig-apperture_problem}


:::{.column-margin}
The **Barber-pole illusion** is an illustration of the aperture problem. The barber pole induces the illusion of downward motion while rotating.

![](figures/optical_flow/barber_pole.png){width="40%"}
:::


### Representation of Optical Flow

We can model motion over time as a sequence of **dense optical flow**
images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) \right]$$ The quantities $u(x,y,t)$and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at image coordinates $(x,y)$ at
time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$. The problem with this formulation
is that we do not have an explicit representation of the trajectory
followed by points in the scene over time. As time $t$ changes, the
location $(x,y)$ might correspond to different scene elements.

An alternative representation is to model motion as a **sparse set of
moving points** (tracks):
$$\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$$ This has the challenge

helical stripes wrapping around the cylinder in a red-white-blue-white pattern
curved 3D arrow floating above the cylinder indicating 'Real motion' (rotation)
straight vertical 3D arrow next to the cylinder pointing downwards indicating 'Observed motion'
aperture plate (semi-transparent overlay with customizable cutouts: circular, vertical slot, horizontal slot)
highlighted tracker point on one of the helix stripes to show local motion
velocity vectors originating from the tracker point: True Motion (horizontal green vector), Normal Motion (perpendicular blue vector), and Perceived Motion (red vector)

interactions.label: Rotation Speed
interactions.teaches: Reversing or accelerating the rotation directly changes the real physical velocity vector, which instantly reverses or speeds up the illusory vertical motion.

interactions.label: Aperture Shape
interactions.teaches: Switches the viewing window boundary, demonstrating how different boundary orientations resolve the motion ambiguity in completely different directions.

demo_steps.title: The Barber-Pole Illusion
demo_steps.narration: Watch the cylinder rotate horizontally (Real motion). Because the stripes are angled, the continuous rotation creates a powerful illusion of downward vertical motion (Observed motion). This is the classic barber-pole illusion.

demo_steps.title: The Local Aperture Problem
demo_steps.narration: By placing a circular aperture over the pole, we hide the cylinder's edges. Without boundary cues, you can only perceive motion perpendicular to the stripe (the blue vector). The true horizontal motion (green vector) becomes completely invisible.

demo_steps.title: Vertical Boundary Cue
demo_steps.narration: Switching to a vertical slot mimic the sides of the actual cylinder. The vertical boundaries force your brain to resolve the ambiguous local motion as a purely vertical downward slide (red vector), reinforcing the illusion.

demo_steps.title: Flipping the Perception
demo_steps.narration: Now look through a horizontal slot. With horizontal boundaries, the exact same physical rotation suddenly appears as purely horizontal motion! This proves that the shape of the aperture dictates the perceived direction of 1D structures.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: Slightly elevated orthographic front view, showing the 3D top of the cylinder clearly while maintaining a broadside view of the helix angles.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant axis is the vertical centerline of the cylinder, running straight up and down on the page. (2) We view the cylinder broadside to clearly see the diagonal stripes on its front face, which implies an azimuth of 0 degrees (looking directly at the cylinder face along the depth axis). (3) The top flat circular cap of the cylinder is visible as a shallow ellipse, showing a clear foreshortening cue. This indicates the camera is elevated above the cylinder, tilting down at an angle of roughly 15 degrees.

camera_view.view_notes: The camera matches the vertical alignment of the source figure, with the top cap of the cylinder visible as an ellipse to establish its 3D geometry.

The aperture plate should be rendered as a dark, semi-transparent overlay (e.g., opacity 0.85) situated slightly in front of the cylinder, with stencil buffer operations used to create clean cutouts for the aperture shapes. Update the velocity vector arrows dynamically based on the rotationSpeed and active apertureType.

evaluation.geometry_accuracy_analysis: The 3D geometry is reconstructed exceptionally well. The rotating barber pole uses a real CylinderGeometry, and the helical stripes are procedurally drawn. The curved 'Real motion' arrow and vertical 'Observed motion' arrow are faithfully represented using 3D Tube, Cylinder, and Cone primitives. Proportions and orthographic viewpoint align tightly with the source.
evaluation.geometry_accuracy_improvement: Shift the observed motion arrow and its label slightly to the right to eliminate overlapping with the cylinder boundary, matching the whitespace distribution of the source.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer built several high-quality, functional, and pedagogically rich interactions: (1) A 'Rotation Speed' slider that alters rotation direction/speed and dynamically scales/reverses the velocity vectors; (2) An 'Aperture Shape' dropdown that modifies the aperture plate geometry and recalculates the normal/perceived motion vectors; (3) Interactive click events on scene objects (cylinder, tracker, arrows, and aperture) displaying educational explanations; (4) A click interaction on the aperture plate itself that cycles through the shapes. A structured step-through demo is coded in JavaScript (goToStep), but no HTML buttons were included in the UI markup to allow users to trigger it.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_improvement: Add next/prev navigation buttons or a step indicator to the HTML UI to make the coded 4-step guided demo accessible to the user.
evaluation.faithfulness_analysis: The rendered model closely matches the source figure's composition, depicting a classic barber pole with red, white, and blue helical stripes, black outlines, and the correct motion labels and arrows. The primary differences are the addition of interactive vector overlays (True, Normal, Perceived) and some minor text overlapping.
discrepancies: Interactive vector arrows and text overlays ('True', 'Normal', 'Perceived') are present on the cylinder but absent in the original.
The 'Observed motion' text label overlaps slightly with the right edge of the cylinder.
UI controls are visible in the bottom-left corner.
evaluation.faithfulness_improvement: Adjust the position offset of the 'Observed motion' label to prevent overlap with the cylinder, and add an option to toggle the extra vector labels for a cleaner match to the source.
evaluation.label_quality_analysis: Source labels: 'Real motion', 'Observed motion'. In the output: 'Real motion' is present but slightly clipped at the top boundary. 'Observed motion' is present but too large and severely overlaps the cylinder. Extra labels 'True', 'Normal', and 'Perceived' are added to explain the vector dynamics, which adds some visual clutter.
evaluation.label_quality_improvement: Decrease the font size of 'Observed motion' and shift its position to the right to prevent overlap with the cylinder.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: The generated figure illustrates the barber-pole illusion and the aperture problem as described in the text. Key concepts taught include: (1) Real horizontal rotation of the cylinder translating into an illusory vertical downward observed motion (Barber-pole illusion). (2) The aperture problem, where local edge orientation limits perceived motion to the perpendicular vector unless boundary cues are present. (3) The resolving effect of different aperture shapes (circular, vertical slot, and horizontal slot) on the perceived motion. The interactive simulation represents these perfectly with three distinct, dynamically updating 3D velocity vectors: True Motion (horizontal, green), Normal Motion (perpendicular to the stripe, blue), and Perceived Motion (varying based on active aperture shape, red). The interactive steps and narrative explanations are highly detailed and mathematically and conceptually correct.
evaluation.notes: The figure is conceptually excellent and features high-quality 3D geometry and interactive simulations of the barber-pole illusion. However, visual quality is held back by overlapping text labels ('Observed motion' overlaps the cylinder) and a hidden step-by-step tutorial that has no controls in the HTML UI.

Shift the 'Real motion' label down slightly or adjust the canvas margins to prevent it from being clipped at the top of the viewport.
Add interactive step navigation buttons ('Previous Step', 'Next Step') to the HTML UI to allow the user to easily progress through the coded 4-step 'Barber-Pole Illusion' tutorial.

The aperture plate should be rendered as a dark, semi-transparent overlay (e.g., opacity 0.85) situated slightly in front of the cylinder, with stencil buffer operations used to create clean cutouts for the aperture shapes. Update the velocity vector arrows dynamically based on the rotationSpeed and active apertureType.

evaluation.geometry_accuracy_analysis: The 3D reconstruction captures all major elements: the barber pole cylinder, the curved top arrow for real motion, and the straight side arrow for observed motion. Geometry is composed of accurate 3D primitives and custom shaders. However, the 'Observed motion' text label and vertical arrow overlap the cylinder, unlike the clean spatial separation in the source image.
evaluation.geometry_accuracy_improvement: Shift the observed motion label and its corresponding arrow further to the right to eliminate overlap with the cylinder geometry.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis:
The developer built several high-quality, functional, and pedagogically useful interactions:
1. **Rotation Speed Slider**: Directly controls the cylinder's rotational velocity, dynamically reversing or accelerating the physical motion and updating the vector lengths/directions in real-time.
2. **Aperture Shape Selector**: Swaps the 3D aperture overlay between 'none', 'circle', 'vertical slot', and 'horizontal slot'. This changes the rendered stencil geometry and updates the perceived motion vector (red arrow) to match the visual illusion.
3. **Interactive 3D Elements**: Clicking on key scene elements (cylinder, arrows, tracker, aperture) displays educational popups or triggers demo transitions (e.g., clicking the aperture cycles through types, clicking the tracker jumps to the relevant demo step).
4. **Guided Step-Through Demo**: A 4-step interactive tour is integrated into the code, utilizing smooth parameter tweening to transition between distinct perceptual states while presenting corresponding text narrations.
evaluation.faithfulness_analysis: The barber pole's colors and striped geometry are highly accurate. However, the layout of the explanatory labels is incorrect. The 'Observed motion' text and down arrow are placed on the left, overlapping the cylinder, instead of on the right. Additionally, the 'Real motion' text label at the top is missing.

evaluation.faithfulness_improvement: Move the 'Observed motion' label and its down-arrow to the right side of the pole, and add the 'Real motion' text label directly above the top curved arrow.
evaluation.label_quality_analysis: The source contains two labels: 'Real motion' (top, with curved arrow) and 'Observed motion' (right side, with down arrow). In the output, 'Real motion' is missing entirely. 'Observed motion' is placed on the left side instead of the right, and its text heavily overlaps the cylinder geometry, reducing readability.
evaluation.label_quality_improvement: Position the 'Observed motion' label to the right side of the cylinder to prevent geometry overlap, and add the missing 'Real motion' text above the top curved arrow.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concept: The aperture problem in optical flow demonstrated via the barber-pole illusion. User-visible claims and representations: (1) 'Real motion' curved arrow and 'Observed motion' vertical arrow are conceptually accurate. (2) Interactive controls for rotation speed and aperture shape are conceptually correct. (3) However, there is a geometric/viewpoint mismatch: the camera is framed from the front (azimuth 0 looking along Z), but the local tracker, vectors, and the aperture plate are positioned on the far right edge of the cylinder (X = radius, Z = 0) and rotated by 90 degrees. This causes the aperture cutouts and local motion vectors to be viewed edge-on (completely flat) from the default camera view, severely undermining the educational clarity of the aperture shapes (circle, vertical/horizontal slots) and their alignment with the front-facing stripes.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_improvement: Reposition the local tracker, velocity vectors, and the aperture plate to the front face of the cylinder (Z = radius, X = 0) and remove the 90-degree Y-rotation of the aperture mesh, so they are viewed flat-on from the default front camera angle.
evaluation.notes: The barber pole's color patterns and interactive aperture simulations are well-implemented, but visual layout discrepancies and a critical viewport/positioning issue with the aperture overlay undermine the overall quality. Specifically, the 'Observed motion' label is on the wrong side and overlaps the cylinder, the 'Real motion' label is missing, and the interactive aperture plate is positioned edge-on to the camera, rendering the slot shapes nearly invisible from the front.
action_items: Move the 'Observed motion' label and its vertical down-arrow to the right side of the cylinder to prevent overlap and match the source layout.
Add the missing 'Real motion' text label directly above the top curved arrow.

Reposition the tracker sphere, local velocity vectors (true, normal, perceived), and the aperture plate to the front face of the cylinder (around Z = pole.radius + offset, X = 0) and adjust their rotations so they are viewed face-on from the default camera angle.
Adjust the top curved arrow's points to make it more clearly curved and three-dimensional, matching the style in the source image.

feedback.rationale: The interactive concept is solid and highly rated, but implementation-level adjustments are needed to fix label positioning, add a missing label, and reposition the aperture plate to face the camera properly.
